tagline: The story of the first exiles to come home from Babylon, the rebuilding of God's temple under Persian rule, and a scribe who called a small, battered people back to the law of Moses.
overview:
Ezra begins where the books of Kings and Chronicles leave off: Jerusalem is in ruins, its temple burned, and the people of Judah scattered in Babylon. Then, in 539 BC, the Persian king Cyrus conquers Babylon, and the next year he allows the exiles to go home and rebuild the house of their God. The first half of the book (chapters 1 to 6) tells how the first returnees, led by Zerubbabel, a descendant of King David, and Jeshua the high priest, set up the altar, lay the temple's foundation, meet years of local opposition, and finally finish the building in 515 BC, prodded by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah.

The second half (chapters 7 to 10) jumps ahead nearly sixty years. Ezra, a priest and a scribe trained in the law of Moses, leads a second group from Babylon to Jerusalem with the backing of King Artaxerxes. He finds that many of the returned exiles, including priests and leaders, have married women from the surrounding peoples, and the book ends with a painful public reckoning over those marriages.

Ezra is a book about what it means to be God's people after the catastrophe. There is no king on David's throne, no independence, and no miracle on the scale of the exodus. There are imperial decrees, building permits, genealogies, and a great deal of paperwork. The book's claim is that God is at work in exactly those things: stirring the heart of a foreign emperor, keeping his promises through prophets, and rebuilding a people around worship and the word of God. It is a small beginning, and the book knows it, but it is a real one.
author:
The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Babylonian Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a), holds that Ezra wrote his own book, and parts of it are plainly his: chapters 7:27 to 9:15 are written in the first person, as Ezra's own memoir. Other parts speak of Ezra in the third person, and the book also contains lists of returnees and official letters in Aramaic, which point to a compiler who gathered and arranged sources.

For much of the modern period scholars treated Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles as one work by a single writer or school, often called the Chronicler, pointing to shared interests (the temple, the Levites, genealogies) and to the fact that the last verses of 2 Chronicles repeat the first verses of Ezra. Since the 1960s and 1970s, scholars such as Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson have argued on linguistic and theological grounds that Ezra-Nehemiah is a separate work from Chronicles, and many now hold that view. Others still see a close relationship. What is not in doubt is that Ezra and Nehemiah were counted as a single book in the Hebrew tradition; the division into two books appears first in Christian tradition and entered Hebrew manuscripts and printed Hebrew Bibles only in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
date:
The events of the book run from Cyrus's decree in 539/538 BC to the marriage reform that follows Ezra's arrival. That arrival is dated to the seventh year of King Artaxerxes (7:7). If this is Artaxerxes I, which is the traditional view and still the most widely held, Ezra came to Jerusalem in 458 BC, thirteen years before Nehemiah. Some scholars argue that the king was Artaxerxes II, which would place Ezra in 398 BC, after Nehemiah; a smaller group proposes reading the thirty-seventh year of Artaxerxes I, about 428 BC. The arguments turn on details such as which high priest was in office and how Ezra and Nehemiah relate in Nehemiah 8 and 12, where they appear together.

The finished book of Ezra-Nehemiah was probably put together in the late fifth or fourth century BC. Its lists of priests reach to a Jaddua and a Johanan (Nehemiah 12:11, 22), which suggests a date no earlier than about 400 BC for the final form.
setting:
Ezra is set in the Persian Empire, the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from Egypt and Asia Minor to the borders of India. The Persians ruled through provinces called satrapies. Judah, now a small province called Yehud, sat inside the great satrapy the Persians called Beyond the River, meaning the lands west of the Euphrates. Its official language was Aramaic, which is why parts of Ezra (4:8 to 6:18 and 7:12-26) are written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.

The Persian kings in the book are Cyrus (who took Babylon in 539 BC), Darius I (522-486 BC), Xerxes (486-465 BC), and Artaxerxes I (465-424 BC). Persian policy generally allowed subject peoples to keep their own gods and temples, and sometimes paid for them, in return for loyalty and taxes. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder now in the British Museum, records Cyrus returning displaced gods and peoples to their homes in Mesopotamia. It does not mention the Jews, but it fits the kind of decree Ezra 1 describes. The returning exiles found a small, poor Judah, surrounded by neighbors in Samaria, Ammon, and elsewhere who had their own claims on the land and their own reasons to resent the newcomers.
purpose: The book was written for the Jewish community in and around Jerusalem after the exile, a people who had come home to a land they did not control and a temple far humbler than Solomon's. It answers their questions. Are we still God's people? Did his promises survive the exile? How should we live now, with no king and a foreign empire over us? Ezra's answer is that God has kept his word through Jeremiah, that the rebuilt temple is truly his house, and that the community's life must now be ordered by the law of Moses. The book also warns: the return from exile does not by itself cure the unfaithfulness that caused the exile, and the community must guard its distinct life with God.
story: Ezra picks up the Bible's story at its lowest point. Second Kings ends with the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC and the exile to Babylon, and Second Chronicles ends with Cyrus's decree, the same words that open Ezra. Ezra tells the first chapters of the return, and Nehemiah continues the account with the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls about 445 BC. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah belong to the years of Ezra 5 and 6, and Malachi probably speaks to the same community some decades later. Esther tells a story of Jews who stayed in Persia during the same era. After Ezra-Nehemiah, the Old Testament's narrative falls silent, and the next chapter of the story opens with the Gospels, some four centuries later, in a Judea under Rome with a temple descended from the one finished in Ezra 6.
christ: Ezra is a book of partial fulfillments. The exiles come home, but they remain subjects of a foreign king. A son of David, Zerubbabel, leads them, but he is a governor, not a king. The temple is rebuilt, but the old men weep because it is so much less than the first (3:12), and nowhere does the book say that God's glory fills it, as it filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple. The prophets of the period, Haggai and Zechariah, look beyond this modest house to a greater glory and a coming king. The New Testament hears those longings answered in Jesus. Matthew's genealogy runs through Zerubbabel (Matthew 1:12-13), John says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and Jesus speaks of his own body as the temple (John 2:19-21). The return under Cyrus is a real act of God's faithfulness, and it is also a signpost toward a deeper return from exile that the book itself does not reach.
reading: Ezra is history written by a believing community, built from sources: lists, royal letters, and Ezra's own memoir. Read it with the documents in mind, and don't skip the lists, which are the book's way of saying that every family and every returnee counted. Watch for the refrain about the hand of God being on Ezra (7:6, 7:28, 8:18, 8:31), which is how the book sees God at work through ordinary events. Notice that the book is not strictly chronological: 4:6-23 jumps forward to later kings to show a pattern of opposition, then 4:24 returns to the reign of Darius. Finally, read chapters 9 and 10 carefully and in context. They are not about ethnicity in the modern sense but about faithfulness to the covenant, and they raise real moral questions that later Scripture, including the book of Ruth, helps a reader think through.

structure.title: The return under Cyrus
structure.summary: Cyrus decrees that the temple be rebuilt and returns its sacred vessels. The first exiles go home, and the book lists them family by family.

structure.title: The temple rebuilt
structure.summary: The returnees set up the altar and lay the foundation, meet opposition that halts the work for years, then resume under the prophets Haggai and Zechariah and finish the temple in the sixth year of Darius, 515 BC.

structure.title: Ezra comes to Jerusalem
structure.summary: Almost sixty years later Ezra the scribe leads a second group from Babylon with a commission from Artaxerxes to teach and apply the law of God, and arrives safely with the temple's gifts.

structure.title: The crisis of the mixed marriages
structure.summary: Ezra learns that many have married women of the surrounding peoples, prays a great prayer of confession, and leads the community in a painful covenant to separate from those marriages.

themes.title: God works through empires
themes.body: Ezra opens with God stirring the spirit of a Persian king, and it keeps returning to royal decrees, letters, and archives. The book's conviction is that the God of heaven rules the kings of the earth, turning their hearts and using their policies to keep his promises to a small people. This is providence without spectacle: no sea parts, but the paperwork comes through.

themes.title: Worship at the center
themes.body: The first thing the returnees build is an altar, and the first great project is the temple. The book lingers over sacrifices, feasts, Levites, singers, and the Passover. The community is being rebuilt around the presence and worship of God, and its identity comes from gathering there rather than from a king or a territory.

themes.title: The word of God rules the community
themes.body: Again and again things are done as it is written in the law of Moses. Ezra himself is introduced as a scribe who studied, practiced, and taught that law (7:10). The book marks a turn in Israel's history toward Scripture as the center of common life, a turn that shaped Judaism and the world into which Jesus was born.

themes.title: A remnant and its faithfulness
themes.body: The returnees see themselves as a remnant, the survivors God has spared. That brings gratitude and also fear, because the sins that caused the exile could return. Ezra's prayer in chapter 9 is a model of corporate confession in which the leader counts himself among the guilty.

themes.title: Opposition and perseverance
themes.body: From chapter 4 onward, every step of rebuilding meets resistance: offers of help with strings attached, discouragement, accusations to the king, forced stoppages. The book is honest that faithful work can stall for years and that God's timing includes long delays.

keyChapters.why: Cyrus's decree fulfills the word spoken through Jeremiah and begins the return from exile, told with echoes of the first exodus.
The altar is rebuilt and the foundation laid, and joy and weeping rise together as the old men remember Solomon's temple.
Darius confirms Cyrus's decree, the temple is finished and dedicated in 515 BC, and the returned exiles keep the Passover.
Ezra is introduced as a scribe devoted to studying, practicing, and teaching the law, and Artaxerxes commissions him.
Ezra's prayer of confession, in which the leader stands with his guilty people, is one of the great prayers of the Old Testament.

parts.body:
Ezra is the fifteenth book of the Bible. It has ten chapters, and it tells how some of the Jewish exiles in Babylon came home to Jerusalem under Persian rule and rebuilt the temple of the LORD, and how, many years later, a priest and scribe named Ezra came to teach them God's law.

The book has two halves. Chapters 1 to 6 begin in 538 BC, when the Persian king Cyrus lets the exiles go home. The first to return build an altar, lay the temple's foundation, meet years of opposition from their neighbors, and finish the house of God in 515 BC, urged on by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. Chapters 7 to 10 jump ahead nearly sixty years. Ezra comes from Babylon with a second group and a letter from King Artaxerxes, and he finds that many of the returned exiles have married women from the peoples around them. The book ends with a painful public reckoning over those marriages.

Some of its scenes stay with readers: a foreign emperor's proclamation, sent because ‘the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia’ (1:1); a crowd at the temple's foundation where ‘The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping’ (3:13); and Ezra on his knees before the house of God, praying for a people whose guilt he counts as his own.

There is no king on David's throne in this book, no independence, and no miracle on the scale of the exodus. There are decrees, letters, building permits, lists of names and a great deal of paperwork. The book's claim is that God is at work in exactly those things. Again and again it says that ‘the hand of the LORD his God was upon him’ (7:6), and it means a king's goodwill, a safe road and a finished house.

It is a small beginning, and the book knows it. But it is a real one.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Ezra begins where the Bible's histories of the kings leave off. Second Kings ends with Jerusalem burned in 587 or 586 BC and the people of Judah carried off to Babylon. Second Chronicles ends with Cyrus's decree, in the same words that open Ezra (2 Chronicles 36:22-23), so that the two books join like links in a chain.

In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah are one book. It stands among the Writings, the third part of the Hebrew Bible, which counts twenty-four books in all. Christian Bibles divide it in two and place it among the books of history, after Chronicles. The division into two books appears first in Christian tradition, and it entered Hebrew manuscripts and printed Hebrew Bibles only in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

Nehemiah carries the story on, about 445 BC, with the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah belong to the years of Ezra 5 and 6, and Malachi probably speaks to the same community some decades later. The book of Esther tells a story of Jews who stayed in Persia in the same era, and its events fall in the gap between Ezra 6 and Ezra 7.

After Ezra and Nehemiah the Old Testament's story falls silent. When it opens again in the Gospels, some four centuries later, Judea is ruled by Rome. The temple that stands in Jerusalem then, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great, descends from the one whose building fills the first half of this book.

parts.h: Who wrote it, and how it was put together
parts.body:
The book does not name its author. A Jewish tradition recorded in the Babylonian Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a) holds that Ezra wrote his own book, and parts of it are plainly his. From 7:27 to the end of chapter 9 Ezra speaks in the first person, in what scholars call the Ezra Memoir. Other parts speak of Ezra in the third person, and the book also holds lists of returnees and official letters, which point to a compiler who gathered and arranged sources.

Some of those sources are in Aramaic, not Hebrew. Aramaic was the common language of the Persian empire's business, and the passages from 4:8 to 6:18 and from 7:12 to 7:26 are mostly official letters to and from the Persian court, quoted in the language the empire used.

For much of the modern period, scholars treated Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles as one work by a single writer or school, often called the Chronicler. They pointed to shared interests, such as the temple, the Levites and family records, and to the way 2 Chronicles ends with the verses that open Ezra. Since the 1960s and 1970s, scholars such as Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson have argued from differences of language and outlook that Ezra and Nehemiah form a separate work from Chronicles, and many now hold that view. Others still see a close relationship.

The finished book of Ezra and Nehemiah was probably put together in the late fifth or the fourth century BC. Its lists of priests reach to a Jaddua and a Johanan (Nehemiah 12:11, 22), which suggests a date no earlier than about 400 BC for its final form.

Christians who receive Ezra as God's word hold more than one of these views, and these notes take no side among them. On every view, the finished book is carefully shaped from its sources.

parts.h: When it happened, and the order of Ezra and Nehemiah
parts.body:
The first half of the book is unusually well dated. Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, and in his first year as its king, 538 BC, he issued his decree (1:1). The altar was rebuilt in the seventh month, probably in 538 or 537 BC (3:1-6), and the foundation was laid in the second year, likely 537 or 536 BC (3:8-10). Then the work stopped. It began again in 520 BC, the second year of Darius I, when Haggai and Zechariah urged the builders on (5:1-2; Haggai 1:1, 15). The temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius (6:15), early in 515 BC, though some count 516.

The second half opens ‘Many years later’ (7:1). Ezra came to Jerusalem ‘in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes’ (7:7). If this is Artaxerxes I, who reigned from 465 to 424 BC, which is the traditional view and still the most widely held, Ezra arrived in 458 BC, thirteen years before Nehemiah. Some scholars, following Albin van Hoonacker in the 1890s, argue that the king was Artaxerxes II, which would place Ezra in 398 BC, after Nehemiah. A smaller group proposes reading the thirty-seventh year of Artaxerxes I, about 428 BC.

The arguments turn on details. Nehemiah 8 and 12 show Ezra and Nehemiah together in Jerusalem. In Ezra 10, Ezra goes to the chamber of ‘Jehohanan son of Eliashib’ (10:6), and the high priest of Nehemiah's day was named Eliashib (Nehemiah 3:1), with a Johanan among his descendants (Nehemiah 12:22-23). A letter from the Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt, dated 407 BC, names a high priest called Johanan in Jerusalem. Scholars who put Ezra after Nehemiah think these are the same man. Others reply that both names were common, and that the chamber may have been named after an earlier Jehohanan.

Careful readers hold each of these views, and these notes take no side. The dates in the timeline below are approximate, and the ones that depend on this debate say so.

Cyrus II, called Cyrus the Great, united the Medes and Persians in the 550s BC, conquered the wealthy kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor, and took Babylon in 539 BC. His empire, named the Achaemenid empire after its royal family, became the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from Egypt and the Aegean Sea to the Indus River.

Persia governed differently from Assyria and Babylon. It divided the empire into large provinces called satrapies, ruled through local leaders, used Aramaic for its business, and allowed, even paid for, the worship of local gods. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder found in the ruins of Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum, records Cyrus returning captured gods to their shrines and letting deported peoples go home. It does not mention the Jews, and it concerns cities in Mesopotamia, but it shows the kind of policy under which the decree of Ezra 1 makes sense.

Judah was now a small province, called Yehud, inside the great satrapy that the book's letters call the region ‘west of the Euphrates’ (5:3). The returned exiles found a small, poor land, with neighbors in Samaria, Ammon and elsewhere who had their own claims on it.

Most of the exiles did not come home. Many had settled in Babylonia, as Jeremiah had told them to (Jeremiah 29:4-7). Clay tablets from a village called Al-Yahudu, which means Judah-town, published in 2014, record Judean families there buying, leasing and paying taxes across several generations.

The kings in Ezra are Cyrus, Darius I (522 to 486 BC), Xerxes (486 to 465 BC) and Artaxerxes I (465 to 424 BC). The book shows their world from the inside: letters in proper official form, royal archives searched, taxes counted, and a king who wanted every people's prayers ‘for the lives of the king and his sons’ (6:10).

The book has two halves, and they are shaped alike. In each, a Persian king gives his permission (chapter 1; chapter 7), a list names the people who went (chapter 2; 8:1-14), gifts for the house of God travel with them, and they arrive and offer sacrifice. Then trouble comes: opposition from outside in the first half (chapter 4), and unfaithfulness from inside in the second (chapters 9 and 10).

Between the two halves lie nearly sixty years, and the story of Esther, set under Xerxes, takes place elsewhere in the empire in that gap.

The book is built from sources, and it does not hide its seams. It gives Cyrus's decree in Hebrew (1:2-4) and again as an archive record in Aramaic (6:3-5). It quotes letters to and from the Persian court in full. In chapter 4 it steps out of the order of time: verses 6 to 23 jump forward to later kings to show that the opposition went on for generations, and verse 24 comes back to the reign of Darius. And from 7:27 to the end of chapter 9, the voice is Ezra's own.

A refrain runs through the second half. ‘The hand of the LORD his God was upon him’ (7:6). ‘The gracious hand of his God was upon him’ (7:9). ‘The hand of our God was upon us’ (8:31). It is the book's way of seeing God at work through ordinary events.

And the book loves lists. They name returnees by family and by town, and priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants, and at the end, the men who had married foreign women. The lists are the book's way of saying that every family counted. The book's last verse is the last line of a list, and nothing comes after it.

The book opens with a date and a promise kept: ‘In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom’ (1:1). Jeremiah had said that Babylon's rule would last seventy years, and that God would then bring his people back (Jeremiah 29:10). Isaiah had named Cyrus as the LORD's shepherd, the king who would say of Jerusalem, ‘She will be rebuilt’ (Isaiah 44:28).

Cyrus's decree calls the LORD ‘the God of heaven’ (1:2), a title used in the Persian period for the supreme god. Persian kings were used to honoring the gods of their subject peoples, and on the Cyrus Cylinder Cyrus credits the Babylonian god Marduk with choosing him. So the decree does not mean that Cyrus became a worshiper of the LORD. The book's point lies elsewhere. Whatever Cyrus thought he was doing, it was the LORD who stirred him.

The same verb comes back four verses later. Family heads, priests and Levites, ‘everyone whose spirit God had stirred’ (1:5), get ready to go. Their neighbors send them off with silver and gold, goods and livestock, as Israel once left Egypt carrying silver and gold from its neighbors. And Cyrus hands back the vessels of the temple that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off to the temple of his own gods. They come home counted, in the care of Sheshbazzar, ‘the prince of Judah’ (1:8).

Chapter 2 names the people who went: their leaders, among them Zerubbabel, a descendant of King David, and Jeshua the priest; their families and their towns; the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants. ‘The whole assembly numbered 42,360’ (2:64), besides servants, singers and animals. The separate figures add up to less than that total, here and in the copy of the list in Nehemiah 7, and the chapter's notes give the explanations scholars offer.

Some families could not prove their descent from Israel, and some priests could not find their names in the records. The priests were not cast off. They were kept from the most holy food ‘until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim’ (2:63), the sacred lots by which God's answer was sought. Their case was left open for God to settle.

parts.h: An altar, a foundation, and a long delay
parts.body:
The first thing the returnees build is not a wall or a house but an altar. In the seventh month the people gather in Jerusalem ‘as one man’ (3:1), set up the altar on its old foundation, and offer the morning and evening sacrifices again, ‘as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God’ (3:2). They keep the Feast of Tabernacles. For about fifty years there had been no regular sacrifice there as the law commanded. By restoring it before anything else, the community says what it is: a people gathered around the worship of the LORD.

In the second year they lay the temple's foundation. The priests blow trumpets, the Levites clash cymbals, and they sing a refrain from the psalms: “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever” (3:11). Then the old men weep. Many of them had seen Solomon's temple, and this beginning was so much smaller. ‘Still, many others shouted joyfully’ (3:12), and no one could tell the joy from the weeping. The book ends its first great scene with both sounds together, and it does not choose between them.

Then the neighbors come. They offer to help, saying, “like you, we seek your God and have been sacrificing to Him since the time of King Esar-haddon of Assyria, who brought us here” (4:2). Zerubbabel and Jeshua refuse. These were peoples the Assyrians had settled in the north after Samaria fell in 722 BC, and Second Kings says of them, ‘these nations worshiped the LORD but also served their idols’ (2 Kings 17:41). Whether the refusal was right is taken up in the notes on chapter 4.

Years of discouragement follow, with counselors hired against the builders and accusations sent to the king. The chapter gathers opposition from about ninety years into one account: under Cyrus and Darius (4:1-5), under Xerxes (4:6), and under Artaxerxes, whose officials warn him that Jerusalem is ‘that rebellious and wicked city’ (4:12), and who orders the rebuilding of the city stopped. The temple itself stood unfinished ‘until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia’ (4:24). Faithful work, the book admits, can stall for years.

parts.h: Prophets, the archives, and a finished house
parts.body:
The work starts again because two prophets speak. In 520 BC Haggai asked the people, “Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” (Haggai 1:4). Zechariah promised that the hands that had laid the foundation would finish the house (Zechariah 4:9). Ezra records it simply: ‘the prophets of God were with them, helping them’ (5:2).

The Persian governor of the province, Tattenai, comes to ask who gave permission for the building. The elders answer him honestly. They tell a foreign official that the first temple fell ‘since our fathers angered the God of heaven’ (5:12), and then they point to Cyrus's decree. Tattenai writes to King Darius and asks for the archives to be searched, and in the meantime ‘the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews’ (5:5), so the work did not stop.

The search finds Cyrus's memorandum, not in Babylon but in the fortress of Ecbatana in Media (6:2), an old capital where the Persian kings spent their summers. Darius confirms it. He orders Tattenai to leave the work alone and to pay for it from the province's taxes, with animals for the sacrifices given daily. The inquiry meant to check the builders ends with the empire funding them.

The house is finished ‘on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius’ (6:15). It is dedicated with joy, and with sacrifices that are modest beside Solomon's, among them twelve goats, ‘one for each tribe of Israel’ (6:17). Then the returned exiles keep the Passover. With them at the meal are ‘all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel’ (6:21). Outsiders who turned to Israel's God were welcome at the table.

One thing is missing. When Solomon's temple was dedicated, ‘the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD’ (1 Kings 8:11). Ezra reports sacrifice, priests in their divisions and great joy, and no cloud. The prophets of those years looked ahead instead. Haggai's word was, ‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former’ (Haggai 2:9).

Only in chapter 7, more than halfway through, does the man the book is named for appear. He is a priest whose family line runs back to Aaron (7:1-5), and he is ‘a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses’ (7:6). A scribe in the ancient world was more than a copyist. Scribes were trained in writing, law and administration, and they served temples and royal courts. In Ezra the word gains a new sense: a scholar of Scripture whose skill lies in understanding and teaching it. The scribes of the Gospels, the experts in the law, look back to him.

One verse gives the heart of the man: ‘For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel’ (7:10). The order matters. Study leads to practice, and practice to teaching.

King Artaxerxes sends him with a letter in Aramaic (7:12-26). It lets any Israelites who wish go with him, sends silver and gold from the king and his counselors for the temple, frees the temple's servants from royal taxes, and gives Ezra authority to appoint judges and to teach God's laws ‘to anyone who does not know them’ (7:25). It sets ‘the law of your God and the law of the king’ side by side (7:26), with heavy penalties for breaking them. Persian kings supported local temples and sometimes gave local laws the backing of the crown, and the letter fits that practice.

Ezra gathers his company by a canal at a place called Ahava, finds no Levites among them, and sends for ministers for the temple (8:15-20). Then he does something unexpected. He had told the king that God's hand protects those who seek him, and so he was ‘ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers’ (8:22). He calls a fast instead, and the people pray. They set out with an enormous treasure, weighed out to the priests and Levites who would carry it, and after about four months on the road it is weighed again in Jerusalem, every piece accounted for (8:33-34).

A few months after Ezra arrives, leaders bring him a report. Many of the returned exiles, priests, Levites and officials among them, have married women from the peoples around them, peoples ‘whose abominations are like those of the Canaanites’ (9:1). The list of peoples is drawn from the law (Deuteronomy 7:1-4; 23:3-8), though most of those Canaanite nations no longer existed in Ezra's day. It names the danger the law had warned of: ‘they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods’ (Deuteronomy 7:4). Solomon's foreign wives had turned his heart (1 Kings 11:1-8), and the prophets had tied the nation's fall to its worship of other gods.

Ezra tears his clothes, pulls hair from his head and beard, and sits in horror until the evening sacrifice. Then he kneels and prays one of the great prayers of confession in the Bible. He had no part in the marriages, yet he prays as one of the guilty people, that ‘our iniquities are higher than our heads’ (9:6), and he ends with nothing to plead: “Here we are before You in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand before You” (9:15).

The people weep with him. A man named Shecaniah proposes a covenant ‘to send away all the foreign wives and their children’ (10:3). An assembly is called, and on a winter day, in heavy rain, the men of Judah and Benjamin sit in the square before the temple and agree. Over three months the cases are heard, town by town, and the book ends with the names of a little over a hundred men who had married foreign women.

This is one of the most troubling scenes in the Old Testament, and it should be read as one. Women and children who had done nothing wrong themselves were sent away, and the text says nothing about what became of them. Readers weigh it in two main ways. Some read the reform as a painful but necessary act of faithfulness at a moment when the small community could have been absorbed into the religions around it, as the northern kingdom had been. They note that the law forbade such marriages, that the peoples are named by their abominations, and that the cases were heard one by one. Others hold that the book records what happened without holding it up as a model, and that the rest of Scripture points another way: Ruth the Moabite, whose God became Israel's God; Isaiah's welcome for ‘the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD’ (Isaiah 56:6); and Malachi, who in the same century tells the men of Judah, ‘do not break faith with the wife of your youth’ (Malachi 2:15). Many readers hold something of both.

Readers also differ over how far these chapters draw a line by birth as well as by faith. Both readings agree that the text is concerned with faithfulness to God, and all agree that it must never be used to justify shutting people out because of their ancestry. The New Testament gives Christians a different instruction for a mixed marriage: if an unbelieving wife is willing to stay, ‘he must not divorce her’ (1 Corinthians 7:12).

Nothing in Ezra 9 and 10 gives anyone today a warrant to break up a marriage or a family.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Ezra
parts.body:
The New Testament says little about Ezra, and it is wise to keep to the few lines it does draw.

It names Zerubbabel, who led the first return, in both family lines of Jesus: ‘Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel’ (Matthew 1:12), and ‘the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel’ (Luke 3:27). The line of David survived the exile in people like those counted in Ezra 2.

The temple of the Gospels is the house finished in Ezra 6, rebuilt and enlarged by Herod the Great. When people in Jerusalem tell Jesus, “This temple took forty-six years to build” (John 2:20), they are speaking of the work Herod began about 20 or 19 BC.

The scribes of the Gospels, the experts in the law, look back to Ezra the scribe. The turn toward Scripture as the center of the people's common life, which begins in this book and in Nehemiah 8, shaped Judaism and the world into which Jesus was born.

And Paul's ruling on mixed marriages goes a different way from Ezra 10. Ezra led men who had married foreign wives to send them away. Paul tells believers not to send away an unbelieving partner who is willing to stay, because ‘the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband’ (1 Corinthians 7:14).

Some Christians have read Ezra, the priest who confessed his people's sins as his own, as a picture of Christ. The New Testament does not draw that line, and these notes do not draw it either. Nothing in the book, or in the New Testament's use of it, is a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people, or on the Samaritans, whose ancestors appear in this book as Judah's neighbors and opponents.

A few habits will help a new reader.

Read it with the documents in mind. It is history written by a believing community from lists, royal letters and Ezra's own memoir. Do not skip the lists. They are the book's way of saying that every family and every returnee counted.

Watch for the hand of God (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31). The book shows almost no miracles, but it keeps saying that God was at work through ordinary events.

Read chapter 4 as a pattern, not a sequence. It gathers opposition from several reigns into one place.

Read the prophets beside the story. Haggai and Zechariah belong inside chapters 5 and 6, and Psalm 126 sings the homecoming of chapters 1 and 2: ‘When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers’ (Psalm 126:1).

Read chapters 9 and 10 slowly and in context, with Ruth, Isaiah 56, Malachi 2 and 1 Corinthians 7 open beside them. They raise real moral questions, and the rest of Scripture helps a reader think them through. They give no one a pattern for breaking up a family today.

And notice how small the book is willing to be. Its temple makes old men weep. Its people are a remnant under a foreign king, and its last chapter ends without a resolution. Zechariah's question fits the whole book: “For who has despised the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10).

hard.line: A Persian king who speaks of the LORD as the God who appointed him to build a temple, and what the Cyrus Cylinder shows.
The vessels counted out add up to 2,499, and the total given is 5,400.
The list of those who came home: its figures add up to less than its total, and differ from the copy in Nehemiah 7.
Families and priests who could not prove their descent, and a question left open for God to settle.
Shouts of joy and loud weeping at the new foundation, and no one could tell them apart.
Who laid the foundation: Zerubbabel and Jeshua (3:8-10), Sheshbazzar (5:16), or the builders of 520 BC (Haggai 2:18)?
Help refused from neighbors who said they worshiped the same God.
A leap forward in time to Xerxes and Artaxerxes, and a letter that stopped the rebuilding of the city.
Darius's threat against anyone who interferes: a Persian king's decree, recorded and not commanded by God.
When Ezra came: 458, 428 or 398 BC, and whether he came before Nehemiah or after.
A foreign king's letter gives Ezra power to enforce God's law with heavy penalties.
Ezra will not ask for soldiers to guard the road, though Nehemiah later travels with them.
‘The holy seed has been mixed’: a line drawn by faith, by birth, or both?
A prayer that confesses the people's guilt as the speaker's own and asks for nothing.
A covenant to send away foreign wives and their children: what the text says, how readers weigh it, and why it gives no one today a warrant to break up a family.
Four men who opposed the plan, or who oversaw it: the Hebrew can be read both ways.
The book ends with a list of names, and with a last verse whose Hebrew is hard to read.

words.line: In Hebrew golah, the exile or the body of exiles. It becomes a name for the returned community, the people carried away and brought back (1:11; 10:8).
The Hebrew ur, to rouse, as one wakes a sleeper. The LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus (1:1) and of everyone who goes up to build (1:5).
A title for the LORD in the Persian period, used in Cyrus's decree (1:2) and in the king's letter to Ezra (7:12, 21, 23).
The Hebrew chesed: faithful, covenant-keeping love, even to the unfaithful. The singers praise it as the foundation is laid (3:11).
The Hebrew yasad, to found, or to restore. Its range helps explain why the book and the prophets speak of the foundation being laid at different times (3:10; 5:16).
In Hebrew netinim, those given: workers given to the temple's service. They came home, and they are listed by family (2:43; 8:20).
The Persian province of which Judah was a small part, the lands beyond the river as seen from Persia (4:10; 5:3).
The Hebrew sopher: an official in charge of documents (4:8), and in Ezra a scholar and teacher of the law of Moses (7:6).

The Hebrew darash, to seek or inquire. Ezra set his heart to seek, that is to study, the law of the LORD (7:10). Later Jewish tradition took its word midrash, interpretation of Scripture, from this root.
The Hebrew yad, hand, meaning power and favor. The refrain says it was on Ezra (7:6, 9, 28) and on his company on the road (8:18, 22, 31).
Two words stand side by side in the king's letter: the law of God, and dat, a Persian word for a king's decree (7:26).
The Aramaic chanukkah. The house of God was dedicated with joy (6:16). The same word later gave its name to Hanukkah, which remembers this temple's rededication in 164 BC.
The Hebrew peletah, those who escaped. Ezra's prayer calls the returned community a remnant spared by grace (9:8, 15).
The Hebrew maal, breaking faith with someone owed loyalty. Ezra 9 and 10 use it to name what the marriages meant (9:2; 10:10).
The Hebrew badal, to separate, the verb of Genesis 1. Outsiders separated themselves from impurity to join Israel (6:21), and the men are told to separate from the peoples of the land (10:11).
The Hebrew miqveh. After Ezra's prayer of utter guilt, it is a layman, Shecaniah, who says ‘there is hope for Israel’ (10:2).

timeline.what: Samaria falls to Assyria, which settles other peoples in the north (2 Kings 17:24). Their descendants are among the neighbors of Ezra 4.
The Babylonians burn Jerusalem and its temple and carry the people of Judah into exile (2 Kings 25).
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon, almost without a fight.
In his first year over Babylon, Cyrus decrees that the house of the LORD be rebuilt, and the first exiles go home (chapters 1 and 2).
The altar is rebuilt in the seventh month, and the Feast of Tabernacles is kept (3:1-6).
The temple's foundation is laid, with shouts of joy and loud weeping (3:8-13).
Opposition and discouragement; the work on the temple stands still (4:4-5, 24).
Darius I takes the Persian throne and spends his first years putting down revolts.
Haggai and Zechariah urge the builders on, and the work begins again in Darius's second year (5:1-2; Haggai 1:1, 15).
The temple is finished on the third day of Adar in Darius's sixth year and dedicated with joy, and the Passover is kept (6:15-22).
Xerxes I reigns. An accusation is lodged against Judah (4:6), and the story of Esther takes place in his court.
Artaxerxes I reigns. His officials persuade him to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (4:7-23).
Ezra comes from Babylon in Artaxerxes' seventh year (7:7-9). In the ninth month the assembly meets in the rain over the marriages (10:9).
Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem as governor in Artaxerxes' twentieth year (Nehemiah 2:1).
Jews at Elephantine in Egypt write to the governor of Judah. Their letter names a high priest Johanan in Jerusalem, a clue in the debate over Ezra's date.
If the king of 7:7 was Artaxerxes II, Ezra came in this year, after Nehemiah.
Ezra and Nehemiah, one book, reach their final form. Their lists of priests run to Jaddua (Nehemiah 12:11, 22).
The temple of Ezra 6, desecrated under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, is rededicated, the origin of Hanukkah.
The Cyrus Cylinder is found in the ruins of Babylon. It is now in the British Museum.
Hebrew manuscripts and printed Hebrew Bibles begin to divide Ezra and Nehemiah into two books, as Christian Bibles long had.

map.title: Judah after the exile, and its neighbors

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: The city of the house of God. The returnees rebuilt the altar here (3:1-3) and finished the temple (6:15), and Ezra arrived in the fifth month (7:8).

places.name: Bethlehem
places.line: David's town. Its men are counted among the first to come home, 123 of them (2:21).

places.name: Bethel
places.line: ‘The men of Bethel and Ai’ came home, 223 of them (2:28).

places.name: Jericho
places.line: Its men are on the list of returnees, 345 of them (2:34).

places.name: Lod
places.line: The town later called Lydda. ‘The men of Lod, Hadid, and Ono’ numbered 725 (2:33).

places.name: Joppa
places.line: The port, today's Jaffa. Cedar logs from Lebanon were brought here by sea for the temple (3:7).

places.name: Samaria
places.line: The province to the north. Peoples the Assyrians had settled ‘in the cities of Samaria’ opposed the rebuilding (4:10), and the king's reply went to his officials there (4:17). Drawn roughly.

places.name: Tyre
places.line: With Sidon, its people were paid in food, drink and oil to bring cedar from Lebanon for the temple (3:7).

places.name: Sidon
places.line: The other port city of Phoenicia. Its people, with those of Tyre, shipped the cedar (3:7).

teaching.mapNote: Only nine places are drawn, each placed elsewhere on this site; Samaria roughly, as a region, and Lod at the point used for Lydda, its later name. Babylon, the Ahava Canal, Casiphia, Ecbatana and Susa lie far to the east and are not placed in this site's records, and most towns of chapter 2 are left off too. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
